From `docs/DESIGN.md:1848` (§10.4). Coalescing runs **when an op is enqueued**, and only against queued ops with the same `target_id`. The doc says this is needed for correctness, not just speed. Without it, an `edit` or `delete` could reach the server for a message it has never seen, causing 404s or "ghost" messages.

| Queued | New op | Result |
|---|---|---|
| `send` | `edit` | Put the new body into the `send`. Only one op remains. |
| `send` | `delete` | **Drop both**, so nothing is sent. |
| `send` | `react` | Keep both, and the react must go after the send. |
| `edit` | `edit` | Keep only the newer edit. |
| `edit` | `delete` | Drop the `edit` and keep the `delete`. |
| `react(add)` | `react(remove)` | Drop both, if the emoji and user are the same. |
| `read(ord=5)` | `read(ord=9)` | Keep the higher `ord`, since only the latest read position matters. |

The table doesn't cover any other pair of ops. The doc says to build this early, because adding it later means checking every op type against every other one.
